intro: Marcelle Meyer plays La cathédrale engloutie, the tenth prelude in Book I of Debussy’s Préludes, about a drowned cathedral. Distant bells rise into a great C-major organ, and the music then sinks beneath the water.

sections.label: A · Open fifths over spaced bass
sections.mNote: Open fifths rise above a widely spaced bass.

sections.label: B · Organ theme in C major
sections.mNote: Thick chords sound above a low C

sections.label: C · Chant theme in C♯ minor
sections.mNote: An earlier phrase returns over a held bass.

sections.label: B′ · Chordal theme returns over quavers
sections.mNote: The chordal theme returns softly above rocking quavers.

sections.label: A″ · Return of the rising fifths
sections.mNote: The rising fifths return; a D sounds within the final chord.

relations.label: The broad melody returns as an echo
relations.basis: Debussy recalls the broad chordal melody in the quieter, lower-register echo section. The matched excerpts lie within the first chordal statement and the echo marked near 268 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.908, sustained 12.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 141.5 s (cache/form/debussy-cathedrale-engloutie.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening, bars 1–6
cues.text: G and D sound across the piano, a wide distance apart. Open fifths rise slowly through the middle register. Debussy marks the opening Profondément calme, deeply calm, with a further direction for a softly ringing mist, and the bass descends while the fifths continue to rise.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Préludes I, no. 10, bars 1–6; Piano Practical Editions, Centenary Edition (2018), p. 67. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/42/IMSLP881620-PMLP2394-Preludes_book_1_.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Breton legend of Ys
cues.text: In the Breton legend, the cathedral of Ys lies beneath the sea. On clear mornings it rises from the water, and bells toll, priests chant and the organ sounds before the building sinks again. Debussy printed its name only after the last bar.
cues.evidence: The legend is summarised in the Centenary Edition, p. 66, and at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_cath%C3%A9drale_engloutie. The title follows bar 89 in the score.

cues.title: Move to B major, bars 14–19
cues.text: The bass moves down from C to B. Under the rising chords the left hand begins triplets, and the harmony moves to B major. Debussy marks the passage Peu à peu sortant de la brume (little by little, emerging from the mist).
cues.evidence: Score, bars 14–19, Centenary Edition, pp. 67–68: bass C–B, triplet accompaniment and Peu à peu sortant de la brume.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chordal passage over low C
cues.text: The piano moves to a G dominant seventh, then sounds a low C beneath a series of full chords. The melody lies inside them, doubled in both hands. At bar 28 Debussy marks Sonore sans dureté (sonorous without harshness), even at fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 22–41, Centenary Edition, pp. 68–69: G dominant-seventh preparation, low C, parallel chords and Sonore sans dureté at bar 28.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the chant, C♯ minor
cues.text: The chords in C major stop. The chant of bars 7–13 returns in C♯ minor, low in the piano, above a held bass (bars 42–61). Debussy marks the passage “Un peu moins lent” and “dans une expression allant grandissant”, and the phrase rises towards a second great chordal crest.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 42–61, Centenary Edition, pp. 70–71: C♯-minor recall of bars 7–13, Un peu moins lent and dans une expression allant grandissant.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Paris Conservatoire admission, 1872
cues.text: On 22 October 1872 Debussy, aged ten, played Moscheles for the jury and won a place at the Paris Conservatoire, one of thirty-three admitted from 157 applicants. In January 1874 his piano teacher Marmontel reported: “Charming child, true artistic temperament; will become a distinguished musician.”
cues.evidence: François Lesure, Claude Debussy: A Critical Biography, trans. and rev. Marie Rolf (University of Rochester Press, 2019), chs. 1–2: admission on 22 October 1872 after auditioning with Moscheles’s Op. 65; Marmontel’s report of 13 January 1874. Publisher’s preview: https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781787444515_A42902130/preview-9781787444515_A42902130.pdf

cues.title: Return of the chordal theme
cues.text: The broad C-major tune returns pianissimo, lower on the keyboard, over rocking quavers. Debussy calls the melody an echo of the phrase heard earlier, and marks the bass flottant et sourd — floating and muffled.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 72–83, Centenary Edition, pp. 71–72: C-major chordal return, Comme un écho de la phrase entendue précédemment, and flottant et sourd.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars in C major
cues.text: The rocking bass stops. Rising fifths recall the opening, now over C. The last chord adds a D to the notes of C major.
cues.evidence: Score, bars 84–89, Centenary Edition, p. 72: Dans la sonorité du début, rising fifths, and final C-major chord with added D.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bass moves from C to B
transitions.from: A · Open fifths over spaced bass
transitions.how: The rising fifths return over a low C. The bass then drops a semitone to B, and the left hand begins rolling triplets under the B-major chords (bars 14–19). Debussy marks the passage as gradually emerging from the mist. The right hand repeats the upward shape of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 14–19, Centenary Edition, pp. 67–68: C–B bass, B-major passage and triplet accompaniment.

transitions.title: G dominant seventh to the organ’s low C
transitions.to: B · Organ theme in C major
transitions.how: The rising figures move from B major through E♭ major to a G dominant seventh, and the left-hand triplets stop. After a broad preparation, a low C sounds beneath the fortissimo melody in parallel chords, played with both hands in the manner of an organist.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 16–28, Centenary Edition, pp. 68–69: B major, E♭ major, G dominant seventh and the C-major chordal statement.

transitions.title: The chant returns in C♯ minor
transitions.from: B · Organ theme in C major
transitions.to: C · Chant theme in C♯ minor
transitions.how: The organ-like chords thin out into widely spaced bell notes. From bar 47 C♯ minor replaces C major, and the chant first heard near the opening returns low in the piano over a held bass. The marking Un peu moins lent begins the next ascent.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 42–53, Centenary Edition, p. 70: bell-like withdrawal and C♯-minor chant from bar 47.

transitions.title: Parallel seventh chords to the C-major echo
transitions.from: C · Chant theme in C♯ minor
transitions.to: B′ · Chordal theme returns over quavers
transitions.how: In bars 61–75 the second climax falls away through parallel seventh chords. A low quaver figure begins to oscillate in the bass, and the earlier C-major melody returns above it, pianissimo. The tune now lies lower in the piano and is marked in the score as an echo.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 61–75, Centenary Edition, p. 71: parallel seventh chords, oscillating bass and quiet C-major return.

transitions.title: The rocking bass stops
transitions.from: B′ · Chordal theme returns over quavers
transitions.to: A″ · Return of the rising fifths
transitions.how: The quaver accompaniment stops on a low C. The piano returns to the rising fifths of the opening, marked Dans la sonorité du début. Slow bell chords continue, and the final C-major chord holds a D within it.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 82–89, Centenary Edition, p. 72: end of the quavers, opening fifths and final added D.

composer.epithet: Composer who trusted his ear over the rules (“pleasure is the law”) and wrote new sounds for the piano, the flute and the orchestra.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and was imprisoned for it. In prison he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on as a pupil. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, described him in January 1874 as “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament”; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Around 1890, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud, he said: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
